preamble: Arabic ẓāʾ ظ [ðˤ] is pronounced as the pharyngealized sibilant [zˤ] in words taken from Literary Arabic into the dialects that lost the dental fricatives. In Egyptian and Levantine Arabic ẓāʾ is /dˤ/ or /zˤ/ depending on the word, and loans from Classical Arabic often have /zˤ/, as in Egyptian ʕaẓīm 'great' (Versteegh 1999, 2000; Retsö 2012: 785–786, cited by Wikipedia). In Egyptian Arabic /zˤ/ appears in borrowings from Literary Arabic, while in inherited words the sound regularly became /dˤ/ (Wikipedia, Egyptian Arabic phonology), and more recent learned borrowings likewise give /s z zˤ/ for /θ ð ðˤ/ (Watson 2002: 22, cited by Wikipedia). In urban Levantine speech ẓāʾ varies between [dˤ] and [zˤ] (Al-Masri 2015; Brustad & Zuniga 2019: 405–407, cited by Wikipedia), and in Modern Standard Arabic it 'can also be' [zˤ] for some speakers (Wikipedia, Ẓāʾ). The fricative becomes a sibilant and keeps its pharyngealization. This is an adaptation of learned vocabulary rather than a regular sound change, and Egyptian ẓābiṭ 'officer' does not belong here, since it comes from ض (Wikipedia, Egyptian Arabic phonology).
